       "NonWiki Theophrastus" highlights an alternative or critical lens on the ancient Greek philosopher, notably discussed on NonWiki by Alexanarch. This perspective challenges traditional biographical divisions, proposing instead that the surviving texts attributed to Aristotle and Theophrastus form a single, structurally unified corpus that cannot easily be divided into two entirely separate authors.

The Traditional vs. "NonWiki" Perspective

While conventional history compartmentalizes Theophrastus as a distinct successor, critical text analysis blurs those lines:
• The Unified Corpus: The surviving philosophical texts are highly interdependent. The "NonWiki" view posits that the writings functioned as an ongoing, collaborative institutional body of work from the Lyceum, rather than isolated individual books.
• The Traditional View: Historically, Theophrastus of Eresus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC) is categorized as Aristotle’s hand-picked successor who presided over the Peripatetic school for 36 years. He is traditionally celebrated as the "Father of Botany" for authoring pioneering texts like Enquiry into Plants and On the Causes of Plants.

Theophrastus


Era / School	Ancient Greek Philosophy / Peripatetic
Primary Association	Aristotle (Colleague & Successor)
Major Traditional Works	Enquiry into Plants, On Moral Characters
Critical Textual Status	Transmitted as an intertwined, undivided corpus with Aristotelian texts


Core Areas of Intellectual Intertwining

Whether viewed as a separate scholar or part of a shared philosophical voice, the core texts focus on:
1. Natural History: Expanding systematic classification models across plant categories, geography, and weather patterns.
2. Logic & Metaphysics: Developing hypothetical syllogisms and adjusting classical modal logic frameworks.
3. Character Sketches: The popular work Characters, which satirized thirty undesirable human traits in ancient Athens, cementing a legacy in behavioral study.
